title: This Planet Orbits Its Star Backward — And Scientists Are Stumped
summary: Imagine a planet going around its star the wrong way — like a rubber duck spinning against the current in a whirlpool. That's exactly what astronomers found! A planet called GJ 3090 b orbits its small red star backward. This is called a retrograde orbit. Normally, planets and stars form from the same spinning disk of gas and dust, so they spin the same way. Changing direction takes a lot of energy. So how did this happen? Scientists looked for a massive companion — like a big planet or a hidden star — that could have yanked the planet into this weird orbit. But they didn't find one. "We may need to think differently about how this system acquired its unusual architecture," said Yann Carteret, an astronomer at the University of Geneva. The team used a telescope in Chile to watch the planet cross in front of its star 10 times. Each time, the starlight dimmed a little. That helped them measure the planet's size and orbit. The star is an M dwarf — small, cool and dim. About three-quarters of the stars in our galaxy are M dwarfs, so studying them is important. The planet orbits its star every 2.9 days and is nearly upside down, tilted 136 degrees. That's similar to Venus in our solar system. One idea: maybe a second disk of gas and dust formed at a different angle and rebuilt the planet's orbit. "The idea that a planetary system could be rebuilt from a second, differently oriented disk is particularly exciting," said co-author Vincent Bourrier. This discovery could change how we think about planet formation.
why_it_matters: This discovery reminds kids that even grown-up scientists can be puzzled, and that asking 'why does this not fit?' is exactly how new ideas about the universe get started.

background_read: Stars and planets are born from the same spinning cloud of gas and dust, which is why almost every planet travels around its star in the same direction the star turns.
M dwarfs (small, cool, dim stars) are the most common stars in our galaxy, and astronomers study them a lot because so many planets have been found around them.
Venus, the planet next door to Earth, is tipped almost completely over — so far over that it spins backwards compared with most planets, a hint that orbits and spins can get twisted over time.
The team in this story works at the University of Geneva (a university in Switzerland) and used a telescope in Chile (a long, narrow country in South America with very clear night skies).
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers including Yann Carteret and Vincent Bourrier, working with a telescope in Chile
WHAT: They found that the planet GJ 3090 b orbits its small red star backward, in a retrograde orbit
WHERE: The star system GJ 3090, studied using a telescope in Chile
WHY: Scientists cannot yet explain the backward orbit, because they found no massive companion that could have pushed the planet into it

perspectives.description: They think this odd planet is a great puzzle and love the idea that a second disk of gas and dust might have rebuilt the planet's orbit at a different angle.
Some may say that one strange planet is not enough proof, and that other explanations need to be tested with more observations.
Because most stars are M dwarfs, people searching for planets say this discovery matters for understanding the many worlds we might find in the future.
